title: Why Cuisine Is a Record of Social History
text:
Nothing feels more natural than what we eat, and few things turn out to be more thoroughly cultural. Every human population faces much the same nutritional requirements, yet what counts as food, as a meal, and as disgusting varies enormously, in patterned ways that anthropologists have tried to account for.

Consider food prohibitions. Some have been read as practical adaptations, since an animal that competes with people for grain, or that is worth more alive, may come to be avoided. Others are better explained by classification. Mary Douglas argued that things are felt to be unclean when they do not fit the categories a culture uses to order the world, so the prohibition concerns conceptual tidiness rather than hygiene. Then there is commensality, the practice of eating together. Who may share a dish, who is served first, who cooks and who is fed: these encode relations of kinship, rank and hospitality more reliably than what people say about themselves. Biology and culture also interact here. Tolerance of milk in adulthood is common in populations with long histories of dairying and uncommon elsewhere, which suggests a practice and a genetic change reinforcing one another over generations. Cuisine is therefore a record of history as much as a matter of taste.
points: Nutritional needs are similar everywhere, but what counts as food and as disgusting varies culturally and in patterned ways.
Some food prohibitions have been explained as practical adaptations, such as avoiding animals more useful alive.
Mary Douglas argued that things are treated as unclean when they do not fit a culture's classifications, so prohibition is about conceptual order, not hygiene.
Commensality, who eats with whom and who is served first, encodes kinship, rank and hospitality.
Adult milk tolerance is common where dairying has a long history, showing culture and biology reinforcing each other.
Cuisine is therefore a record of a society's history rather than simply a matter of taste.
